lines.text: The Netherlands has many public holidays [feestdagen] and special days.
The most important ones, in order through the year:
Valentine's Day [Valentijnsdag], 14 February: the day of love.
People send each other a card or give a small gift.
Carnival [Carnaval] (three days, from Sunday through Tuesday in February or March, a different date each year): people put on funny costumes, go dancing and usually drink a lot of beer.
Mainly in the south [zuiden] of the Netherlands.
Around this date schools have their spring break [voorjaarsvakantie].
Easter [Pasen], a Sunday and Monday in March or April: Christians celebrate that Jesus lives again.
It is also a spring festival [lentefeest].
People eat lots of eggs [eieren], including chocolate ones.
Almost everyone has an extra day off on the Monday.
Eid al-Fitr, also known as "Sugar Feast" [Suikerfeest]: a celebration for Muslims after Ramadan, a month of fasting [vasten].
They eat many sweet things.
King's Day [Koningsdag], 27 April: the birthday [verjaardag] of the king.
There are markets where everyone may sell second-hand [tweedehands] items.
Everything on the streets is orange [oranje] and many people hang a flag outside.
For most Dutch people an important day off.
Remembrance of the Dead [Dodenherdenking], 4 May: at 8:00 pm everyone is silent for two minutes [twee minuten stil].
People remember all those who died [overleden] in a war [oorlog].
In the evening the flag hangs at half-mast [halfstok] — only on 4 May.
Liberation Day [Bevrijdingsdag], 5 May: we celebrate the end of the Second World War [Tweede Wereldoorlog] in the Netherlands in 1945.
5 May is a day off once every five years [één keer in de vijf jaar].
Around this date there is the May school holiday.
On 4 and 5 May we think about our freedom [vrijheid].
Mother's Day [Moederdag], second Sunday in May, and Father's Day [Vaderdag], third Sunday in June: mothers and fathers receive small gifts.
Ascension Day [Hemelvaart], a Thursday in May: Christians celebrate that Jesus went to heaven [hemel].
Most people have the day off.
Pentecost [Pinksteren], a Sunday and Monday in May or June: Christians celebrate that God came into people.
Extra day off on the Monday.
Keti Koti (1 July): day of freedom [vrijheid], the end of slavery [slavernij].
People wear traditional [traditionele] Surinamese clothes and dance.
It used to be only a Surinamese celebration; now more people celebrate it.
Sinterklaas (5 December, especially in the evening): the birthday of Sinterklaas (as children believe).
People give presents, especially to children.
Christmas [Kerstmis], 25 and 26 December: Christians celebrate that Jesus was born.
It is a winter celebration: many people put up a Christmas tree [kerstboom] at home and make nice food.
Around this date there is the Christmas school holiday.

New Year's Eve and New Year [Oud en nieuw] (oudjaar 31 December, nieuwjaar 1 January): 31 December is a cozy evening, there is sometimes fireworks [vuurwerk] and people eat Dutch doughnut balls [oliebollen].
The Dutch flag [vlag] has the colors red, white and blue [rood, wit en blauw].
On Koningsdag people often add an orange pennant [oranje wimpel].
The Dutch national anthem [volkslied] is called 'het Wilhelmus'.
People sing it on Koningsdag, on 4 and 5 May, and at sports matches, for example when the Dutch national football team [Nederlands elftal] plays.
Not everyone celebrates all holidays.
For people without religion, Christian holidays are not so important.
On Christian holidays almost everyone has the day off; sometimes shops are closed.

People usually celebrate holidays at home [thuis], with family and sometimes friends, but you notice [merkt] the holiday almost everywhere: in shops, on the street, at schools and at work (for example little lights [lichtjes] and Christmas music for Kerstmis).
